name: Two-Ply

stars.name: Ply Major
stars.notes: Larger of a contact-close red pair; the two stars trade material across a shared stream visible in every long exposure.

stars.name: Ply Minor
stars.notes: Twin ember separated from its partner by barely 0.06 AU; together they spin once every eleven hours, the tightest known binary in the Shallows.

planets.name: Twistroot
planets.notes: Circumbinary P-type orbit skimming the pair's roche limits; the combined tide has kneaded it into a cracked, airless lump.

planets.name: Doubleface
planets.notes: P-type orbit; tidally locked with a narrow twilight ring where survey drones recorded faint prebiotic chemistry before funding lapsed.

planets.name: Endnote
planets.notes: Cold outermost P-type body; its perfectly circular orbit is the one feature here that refuses to match the system's chaotic models.

anomalies.name: The Grafting Loom
anomalies.location: threaded between the stellar pair and orbit 1
anomalies.notes: A filamentary mass concentration binds the two dwarfs tighter than their visible matter allows; probes that cross the threads return with clocks and fuel gauges quietly disagreeing.

faction_control.notes: Unclaimed and unvisited by any registry authority; the nearest corporate charter lists it as a navigation hazard rather than a system.

history: First flagged as an impossible photometric flicker in a transit catalog, the tight pair was confirmed by a single flyby probe that promptly lost attitude control near the inner orbits.
A research consortium's follow-up expedition measured orbital decay far faster than tidal models permitted, publishing the dark-matter filament hypothesis that gave the anomaly its name.
Funding for further study lapsed after two instrument packages went silent inside the filament zone, and the system has sat empty ever since.
description: Two red dwarfs turn about one another at a distance of six stellar diameters, so close that a bridge of stolen plasma arcs between them, spinning the pair like thread winding onto a spindle. Three small planets circle the coupled fires in compact circumbinary orbits, each locked or kneaded into strange permanence. Beyond them lies only cold and a single tiny ice world on an unnaturally perfect circle.

No flag flies here and no station lights the dark; even salvage crews give the system a wide berth. The only visitors are the occasional automated probe lofted by distant universities to re-measure an orbital decay nobody can explain. Whatever traffic exists passes through rather than to, and does so quickly.

The Grafting Loom's invisible threads hold the stars closer than physics politely allows, and instruments that graze them come back telling two different stories. The last human expedition logged a fourteen-second discrepancy in its own mission clocks and declined to investigate. Somewhere in that woven dark, Endnote's too-perfect orbit waits for someone brave, foolish, or funded enough to ask why.
